body: The trachea is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the tubular airway connecting the larynx to the main bronchi. Parameters: (1) the cartilaginous framework — approximately 16-20 C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings, open posteriorly and connected by the trachealis muscle; (2) the mucosal lining — pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells that propel trapped particles upward via the mucociliary escalator; (3) the length and position — approximately 11 cm long in adults, extending from the larynx at the level of C6 vertebra to the carina at T4-T5 where it bifurcates; (4) the blood supply — supplied by the inferior thyroid arteries and drained by the thyroid venous plexus, innervated by the vagus and sympathetic trunks. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, emergency airway management protocols, and thoracic surgery references. e.g.: the trachea described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; tracheostomy tube placement through the anterior tracheal wall in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; tracheal bifurcation visualized on a PA chest radiograph | not: the bronchus (the tubular airway below the tracheal bifurcation, a distinct structure); the larynx (the structure above the trachea housing the vocal folds, a distinct structure) [formal: trachea | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The thyrohyoid membrane is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the fibrous band joining the superior border of the thyroid cartilage to the body and greater horns of the hyoid bone, suspending the larynx from the hyoid. Parameters: (1) the boundaries - superiorly the hyoid body and greater horns, inferiorly the superior border and angle of the thyroid cartilage; (2) the composition - a thin fibrous sheet, its median portion thicker and continuous with the midline raphe, its oblique lateral portions thinner; (3) the relations - the superior laryngeal vessels and the internal laryngeal nerve pierce its oblique portion, and the cricothyroid muscle inserts on the thyroid cartilage below it; (4) the clinical significance - a landmark for the midline laryngofissure and laryngocelectomy approaches, a route for laryngeal suspension, and a visible indicator of laryngeal position on lateral neck radiograph. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts and head-and-neck surgery references. e.g.: the thyrohyoid membrane described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; the superior laryngeal vessels piercing the oblique thyrohyoid membrane in cadaveric dissection; the thyrohyoid membrane split in a midline laryngofissure for laryngocelectomy | not: the cricothyroid membrane (the sheet below, between thyroid and cricoid); the hyoepiglottic ligament (the median band fixing the epiglottic tip to the hyoid body) [formal: membrana thyrohyoidea | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The thyroepiglottic ligament is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the fibrous band connecting the apex and lateral borders of the epiglottis to the anterior surface of the thyroid cartilage, specifically to the angle of the thyroid lamina just below the superior laryngeal nerve. Parameters: (1) the attachments — the epiglottic apex and lateral margins connected to the thyroid angle; (2) the composition — dense fibrous connective tissue, continuous with the pre-epiglottic space fat anteriorly; (3) the functional role — maintains the position of the epiglottis relative to the thyroid cartilage and transmits forces during swallowing. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, laryngology references, and surgical atlases. e.g.: the thyroepiglottic ligament described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake; the thyroepiglottic ligament as a surgical landmark in thyroepiglottoplasty per Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; the thyroepiglottic ligament visualized during microlaryngeal surgery in Miller's Anesthesia, 9th edition | not: the hyoepiglottic ligament (distinct ligament to hyoid bone); the pre-epiglottic space (fat-filled space anterior to the epiglottis) [formal: ligamentum thyroepiglotticum | substrate: matter | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The laryngeal surgical landmark is a human-made surgical construct mapping the physical sites in the larynx used as reference points during airway surgery. Parameters: (1) the anatomical location; (2) the surgical relevance; (3) the identification technique. It persists as a procedural step in laryngeal surgery. e.g.: the laryngeal surgical landmark identified in tracheostomy; the laryngeal surgical landmark used in laryngotracheal separation | not: the laryngeal anatomical landmark [formal: landmarkum laryngeus | substrate: matter | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

The thyrohyoid membrane is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the broad fibrous sheet extending between the superior border of the thyroid cartilage and the hyoid bone. Parameters: (1) the attachments — inferiorly attached to the superior border and superior horns of the thyroid cartilage, superiorly to the superior margin and tips of the greater horns of the hyoid bone; (2) the composition — a broad fibrous sheet with a thicker anterior margin and thinner posterior portions; (3) the relationships — anteriorly continuous with the infrahyoid musculature, posteriorly opens into a slit-like interval (the thyrohyoid hiatus) through which the internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal vessels pass; (4) the lateral thickening — the lateral margins thicken into the thyrohyoid ligament, which provides the primary structural connection between the hyoid and thyroid cartilages; (5) the clinical access — a landmark for the thyrohyoid membrane puncture technique in percutaneous tracheostomy and a surgical approach window in anterior neck dissection. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, head and neck surgical atlases, and airway management guidelines. e.g.: the thyrohyoid membrane described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; the thyrohyoid membrane as a surgical landmark in anterior neck dissection per Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; percutaneous tracheostomy via thyrohyoid membrane puncture in the journal of Critical Care Medicine [formal: membrana thyrohyoidea | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The salpingopharyngeus muscle is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the paired longitudinal muscle of the pharynx originating from the cartilaginous part of the auditory tube, whose fibers merge with the palatopharyngeus to form the salpingopharyngeal fold and elevate the pharynx during swallowing. Parameters: (1) the origin — the cartilaginous portion of the auditory (Eustachian) tube near the torus tubarius; (2) the course — descends along the lateral pharyngeal wall as a narrow muscular band, blending inferiorly with the palatopharyngeus muscle; (3) the insertion — posterior border of the thyroid cartilage and the pharyngeal wall; (4) the action — elevates the pharynx and larynx during swallowing and speech; (5) the clinical significance — forms the salpingopharyngeal fold visible on nasopharyngoscopy, landmark for identifying the auditory tube opening in nasopharyngeal carcinoma staging, relevant in pediatric adenoidectomy. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in otolaryngology, cranial nerve assessment, and nasopharyngeal disease evaluation. e.g.: salpingopharyngeus muscle in Gray's Anatomy as part of the palatopharyngeal complex; salpingopharyngeal fold visualized during nasopharyngoscopy; salpingopharyngeus function in pharyngeal elevation during swallowing assessed by videofluoroscopy | not: the palatopharyngeus-muscle (the adjacent muscle blending with it, a distinct muscle); the auditory-tube (the cartilaginous structure providing origin, not the muscle itself); the levator-veli-palatini (another muscle associated with the auditory tube, innervated differently) [formal: musculus salpingopharyngeus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The nasopharynx is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the superior division of the pharynx, lying posterior to the nasal cavity and superior to the soft palate, forming the airway conduit between the nasal choanae and the oropharynx. Parameters: (1) the boundaries — anteriorly the posterior nasal apertures (choanae), inferiorly the superior border of the soft palate, posteriorly the mucosa overlying the body of the sphenoid and the superior constrictor muscle; (2) the lymphoid tissue — the pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid) on the posterior wall, and the lateral pharyngeal recess (fossa of Rosenmüller) on each lateral wall; (3) the epithelial lining — pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium continuous with the nasal cavity; (4) the clinical relevance — site of adenoid hypertrophy causing nasal obstruction, and the fossa of Rosenmüller as a common site for nasopharyngeal carcinoma. It persists as a standard anatomical region in human anatomy texts, otolaryngology, and head-and-neck radiology. e.g.: the nasopharynx shown in the pharynx chapter of Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; nasopharyngoscopy for adenoid evaluation per Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; nasopharyngeal carcinoma staging using the pharyngeal recess on MRI per AJCC 8th edition | not: the oropharynx (the middle division of the pharynx behind the oral cavity, inferior to the soft palate); the nasal cavity (the air-filled space anterior to the nasopharynx, separated by the choanae); the pharyngeal tonsil (the lymphoid tissue within the nasopharyngeal wall, a structure contained within the space) [formal: nasopharynx | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The esophagus is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the muscular conduit extending from the lower pharynx at the level of the cricoid cartilage (C6) to the stomach through the diaphragmatic hiatus (T10), whose primary function is transporting ingested material from the pharynx to the gastric lumen. Parameters: (1) the segments — cervical (C6 to thoracic inlet), thoracic (thoracic inlet to diaphragm), and abdominal (diaphragm to stomach); (2) the wall layers — mucosa (stratified squamous epithelium), submucosa with esophageal glands, muscularis externa (upper third skeletal muscle, middle third mixed, lower third smooth muscle), and adventitia; (3) the constrictions — four anatomical narrowings at the pharyngoesophageal junction, crossing of the aortic arch and left main bronchus, and esophageal hiatus, which are sites of foreign body impaction; (4) the clinical significance — gastroesophageal reflux disease, Barrett esophagus, esophageal varices, achalasia, and esophageal cancer staging. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, gastroenterology, and thoracic surgery. e.g.: the esophagus as described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; esophageal manometry study in a patient with achalasia per the ACG guidelines; endoscopic visualization of Barrett esophagus in a gastroenterology case report | not: the trachea (the airway tube above, distinct from the alimentary esophagus); the larynx (the voice organ above, distinct from the esophageal conduit) [formal: oesophagus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The corniculate cartilages (cartilagines corniculatae) are a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the paired conical cartilages that sit atop the apices of the arytenoid cartilages within the larynx, forming part of the posterior laryngeal inlet and supporting the aryepiglottic folds. Parameters: (1) the position — each cartilage rests on the apex of its corresponding arytenoid cartilage; (2) the composition — elastic cartilage, continuous with the arytenoid's cartilage; (3) the relationships — embedded within the aryepiglottic fold, adjacent to the cuneiform cartilage, and contributing to the closure of the laryngeal inlet during swallowing. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, laryngology references, and airway management guides. e.g.: the corniculate cartilage shown in the larynx chapter of Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake; the corniculate tubercle identified during direct laryngoscopy per Miller's Anesthesia, 9th edition; corniculate cartilage calcification noted on lateral neck radiograph in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition | not: the cuneiform cartilage (paired wedge-shaped cartilage in the aryepiglottic fold, anterior to the corniculate); the arytenoid cartilage (larger pyramid-shaped cartilage the corniculate rests upon, a distinct structure); the epiglottis (leaf-shaped cartilage forming the anterior roof of the laryngeal inlet, a distinct structure) [formal: cartilago corniculata | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The inferior pharyngeal constrictor is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the lowest and broadest band of muscle forming the posterior and lateral walls of the inferior pharynx. Parameters: (1) the origins - the oblique and transverse parts arising from the cricoid cartilage (thyrocricoid membrane and posterior lamina) and the thyroid cartilage (oblique line); (2) the insertion - the pharyngeal raphe posteriorly where fibers from both sides interdigitate; (3) the fiber arrangement - lower fibers run horizontally to the raphe, upper fibers (cricopharyngeus part) run obliquely upward and medially, forming the lower boundary of the inferior constrictor; (4) the apertures - the esophagus passes through inferiorly at the pharyngoesophageal junction, the internal laryngeal nerve pierces between the superior and inferior bands, and the superior laryngeal artery passes through the same gap; (5) the clinical significance - the cricopharyngeus part forms the upper esophageal sphincter (Cricopharyngeal dysfunction causes dysphagia and Zenker's diverticulum through Killian's dehiscence between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus parts. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, otolaryngology references, and swallowing assessment protocols. e.g.: the inferior pharyngeal constrictor in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake; the cricopharyngeal bar seen on barium swallow per Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; Killian's dehiscence at the thyropharyngeus-cricopharyngeus junction in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition | not: middle-pharyngeal-constrictor (intermediate band from hyoid, distinct layer); superior-pharyngeal-constrictor (uppermost band from pterygoid, distinct layer); cricopharyngeus-muscle (the transverse band forming the upper esophageal sphincter, a specialized part of this muscle) [formal: constrictor pharyngis inferior | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The cricotracheal membrane attachment is a human-made surgical construct mapping the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage to the superior border of the first tracheal ring, used as a landmark during tracheostomy. Parameters: (1) the anatomical anchor points; (2) the fibrous tissue bridge; (3) the surgical exposure technique. It persists as a procedural step in airway management protocols. e.g.: the cricotracheal membrane attachment identified in ATLS tracheostomy protocol; cricotracheal membrane attachment dissected in laryngotracheal separation surgery | not: the cricothyroid membrane attachment [formal: membrana cricotrachealis | substrate: matter | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

The superior laryngeal nerve is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the branch of the vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) that divides into internal and external divisions to supply the larynx above the level of the vocal folds. Parameters: (1) the origin — arises from the inferior vagal ganglion as the vagus nerve passes the inferior ganglion of the inferior salivary nucleus in the jugular foramen; (2) the internal branch — pierces the thyrohyoid membrane to become the internal laryngeal nerve, providing sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds; (3) the external branch — descends on the inferior pharyngeal constrictor to supply the cricothyroid muscle and the superior laryngeal muscles; (4) the anatomical course — travels with the superior laryngeal artery along the thyrohyoid membrane. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, laryngology references, and regional anesthesia protocols. e.g.: the superior laryngeal nerve described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; superior laryngeal nerve block for laryngeal surgery in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve tested during sensory evaluation of the larynx | not: the recurrent laryngeal nerve (the other laryngeal branch supplying the larynx below the vocal folds); the vagus nerve (the parent nerve from which the superior laryngeal nerve branches, a distinct structure) [formal: nervus laryngeus superior | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The stylopharyngeus muscle is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the paired longitudinal muscle of the pharynx originating from the styloid process, whose unique course passes between the superior and middle pharyngeal constrictors to elevate the pharynx and larynx during swallowing and speech. Parameters: (1) the origin — apex of the styloid process and its associated stylohyoid ligament; (2) the course — descends along the lateral pharyngeal wall, passing between the superior and middle constrictor muscles to insert into the posterior border of the thyroid cartilage; (3) the innervation — glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), the only pharyngeal muscle with this innervation; (4) the action — elevates the pharynx and larynx during swallowing and speech, widens the pharyngeal cavity; (5) the clinical significance — landmark in tonsillectomy surgery, its atrophy assessed in glossopharyngeal nerve palsy, and its course relevant to transstyloid surgical approaches to the parapharyngeal space. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in head-and-neck anatomy, otolaryngology, and cranial nerve assessment. e.g.: stylopharyngeus described in Gray's Anatomy as sole muscle between constrictors; stylopharyngeus course between constrictors visualized during tonsillectomy; glossopharyngeal nerve palsy assessed via stylopharyngeus-mediated pharyngeal elevation | not: the stylohyoid-muscle (the digastric-related muscle also from the styloid process, innervated by CN VII); the superior-pharyngeal-constrictor (a constrictor muscle, not a longitudinal elevator); the glossopharyngeal-nerve (the nerve that innervates this muscle, not the muscle itself) [formal: musculus stylopharyngeus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The laryngeal framework is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the complete cartilaginous scaffold of the larynx — the thyroid, cricoid, and epiglottic cartilages with the paired arytenoid and corniculate cartilages, joined by the thyrohyoid, cricothyroid, cricotracheal, and thyroepiglottic ligaments and membranes — as one structural unit. Parameters: (1) composition — the six cartilages (thyroid, cricoid, epiglottis, two arytenoids, two corniculati) with the inter-cartilaginous ligaments and membranes that fix their relations; (2) function — the anchor for the intrinsic laryngeal muscles at the arytenoid muscular processes and the thyroid laminae, the suspension of the vocal folds, and the maintenance of the airway lumen against collapse; (3) clinical access — the framework is the operative field of laryngofissure, medialization thyroplasty, and total laryngectomy, and its articulations are the joints moved in arytenoid adduction and abduction. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, laryngology atlases, and airway surgery references. e.g.: the laryngeal framework diagrammed in the larynx chapter of Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake; the framework exposed during laryngofissure in an airway management procedure per Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; the framework of a total laryngectomy specimen in an ENT surgery atlas | not: the thyroid cartilage alone (a single member of the framework, not the whole); the cricoid cartilage alone (a single member); the laryngeal inlet (the opening bounded by the framework, not the framework itself) [formal: armatura laryngis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The stylohyoid ligament is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the band of fibrous tissue connecting the styloid process of the temporal bone to the greater horn of the hyoid bone, suspending the hyoid from the skull base. Parameters: (1) the attachments - the styloid process of the temporal bone superiorly, the greater horn of the hyoid bone inferiorly; (2) the structure - a flat fibrous band approximately 3 cm long through which the stylohyoid muscle passes, the ligament remaining behind it; (3) the function - transmitting force between the skull base and the hyoid and limiting hyoid excursion during swallowing and mastication; (4) the clinical significance - calcification and elongation of the ligament and styloid process producing the pain of Eagle syndrome. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, skull-base surgical references, and radiology. e.g.: the stylohyoid ligament depicted in the skull chapter of Moore Clinically Orientated Anatomy, 9th edition; stylohyoid ligament calcification on lateral skull radiograph in Eagle syndrome in a radiology teaching file; the stylohyoid ligament preserved in a parotidectomy approach in a head and neck surgery atlas | not: the stylohyoid muscle (the muscle passing through the ligament, a distinct structure); the styloid process (the bone to which the ligament attaches); the temporomandibular joint (the mandibular articulation, a different relation) [formal: ligamentum stylohyoideum | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The hyoid bone is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the U-shaped bone suspended above the laryngeal framework, the only bone of the human body not directly articulated to any other. Parameters: (1) the parts — a central body with a paired greater horn and a paired lesser horn; (2) the suspensions — held by the stylohyoid ligament, the thyrohyoid membrane below, and the muscles of the tongue and pharynx, so that it floats rather than joints; (3) the relations — the superior border of the thyroid cartilage connects to its body by the thyrohyoid membrane; the epiglottic apex is fixed to its body by the hyoepiglottic ligament; the root of the tongue attaches beneath the body; (4) the clinical significance — a fracture of the hyoid body is a marker of severe blunt neck trauma, and the bone is the surface landmark for palpating the larynx. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, maxillofacial radiology, and forensic references. e.g.: the hyoid bone as depicted in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; the hyoid bone fracture assessed on lateral neck radiograph in blunt neck trauma; the hyoid bone's position marked on a lateral cephalometric radiograph in Miller's Anesthesia | not: the thyroid cartilage (a laryngeal cartilage below the hyoid, a separate structure); the thyroid gland (the endocrine organ anterior to the larynx) [formal: os hyoideum | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The superior pharyngeal constrictor is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the quadrate sheet of muscle forming the uppermost band of the posterior and lateral walls of the pharynx. Parameters: (1) the origins - pterygoid hamulus, pterygomandibular raphe (shared with the buccinator), and the medial pterygoid plate of the sphenoid bone; (2) the insertion - the pharyngeal tubercle of the occipital bone and the pharyngeal raphe, a midline tendon where the fibers of both sides interdigitate; (3) the fiber orientation - lower fibers run inferiorly, upper fibers overlap the middle constrictor; (4) the aperture - the stylopharyngeus nerve passes through between the superior and middle bands; (5) the clinical significance - landmark for pharyngeal surgery, origin of superior constrictor palsy in stroke, and site of pharyngoplasty for velopharyngeal insufficiency. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, otolaryngology references, and swallowing assessment protocols. e.g.: the superior pharyngeal constrictor in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake; the pharyngeal raphe during constrictor repair in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; stylopharyngeus nerve passing through the constrictor in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition | not: the middle-pharyngeal-constrictor (the intermediate band arising from the hyoid bone, a distinct muscle layer); the inferior-pharyngeal-constrictor arising from the cricoid and thyroid cartilages, a distinct muscle layer; the buccinator (the facial muscle sharing the pterygomandibular raphe, not a pharyngeal muscle) [formal: constrictor pharyngis superior | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The middle pharyngeal constrictor is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the fan-shaped sheet of muscle forming the intermediate band of the posterior and lateral walls of the pharynx. Parameters: (1) the origins - the lesser and greater horns of the hyoid bone and the hyoidothyroid ligament; (2) the insertion - the pharyngeal raphe and overlapping fibers posteriorly where it fuses with the superior constrictor above and the inferior constrictor below; (3) the fiber arrangement - fibers fan superiorly to overlap the superior constrictor and inferiorly to be overlapped by the inferior constrictor; (4) the aperture - the stylopharyngeus muscle passes between the superior and middle constrictors, and the glossopharyngeal nerve and tonsillar artery pass between the middle and inferior constrictors; (5) the clinical significance - landmark in tonsillectomy (the constrictor is the bed from which the tonsil is dissected), site of pharyngeal diverticula, and reference for pharyngeal pacing. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, otolaryngology references, and swallowing assessment protocols. e.g.: the middle pharyngeal constrictor in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake; the tonsil bed defined by the middle constrictor in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; stylopharyngeus passing between the constrictors in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition | not: superior-pharyngeal-constrictor (uppermost band from pterygoid, distinct layer); inferior-pharyngeal-constrictor (lowest band from cricoid/thyroid, distinct layer); stylopharyngeus (passes between constrictors, not a constrictor) [formal: constrictor pharyngis medius | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The cuneiform cartilage is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the paired nodular elastic cartilages embedded within the substance of the aryepiglottic folds, situated between the corniculate cartilages posteriorly and the lateral margins of the epiglottis anteriorly. Parameters: (1) the position — embedded within the aryepiglottic fold mucosa, lateral to the corniculate cartilage and superior to the arytenoid apex; (2) the composition — elastic cartilage core surrounded by mucous glands and fibroelastic connective tissue; (3) the variability — absent in approximately 25% of individuals (WSN cuneiformis), making its presence a positive anatomical finding on endoscopy; (4) the functional role — stiffens the aryepiglottic fold and contributes to the sphincteric closure of the laryngeal inlet during swallowing. It persists as a standard anatomical variant in human anatomy texts, laryngology atlases, and head and neck radiology. e.g.: the cuneiform cartilage described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; cuneiform cartilage visible as a nodule on direct laryngoscopy; identification of the cuneiform cartilage on axial CT imaging | not: the corniculate cartilage (sitting atop the arytenoid apex, not embedded in fold mucosa); the aryepiglottic fold (the mucosal fold that contains the cuneiform cartilage, a distinct structure) [formal: cartilago cuneiformis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The tracheal cartilage is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the stacked C-shaped hyaline rings that form the cartilaginous framework of the trachea. Parameters: (1) number and shape — approximately 16-20 rings, each an incomplete C-shaped plate of hyaline cartilage, open posteriorly; (2) position — the rings stack from just below the cricoid cartilage to the level of the carina (T4-T5), separated by short intervals of fibrous membrane; (3) posterior completion — the open posterior gap of each ring is bridged by the trachealis muscle and the membranous posterior wall, which allows esophageal distension; (4) function — the rings keep the lumen patent against negative intrathoracic pressure while their incomplete shape preserves flexibility; (5) clinical role — landmarks for tracheostomy (typically the second to third rings), for tracheal resection and reconstruction, and the source of the calcified rings seen on chest radiographs. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, thoracic surgery references, and airway management protocols. e.g.: the tracheal cartilage rings described in the trachea chapter of Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; tracheostomy incision between the second and third tracheal rings per Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; the tracheal rings calcified on a PA chest radiograph | not: the cricoid cartilage (the single complete ring above the trachea, a laryngeal cartilage); the trachealis muscle (the smooth muscle spanning the posterior gap, not cartilage); the bronchial cartilages (the irregular plates of the bronchi below the carina) [formal: cartilago trachealis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The paraglottic space is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the potential fat-filled compartment on each side of the larynx, bounded medially by the perichondrium of the thyroid lamina and laterally by the thyrohyoid membrane, extending from the hyoid to the cricoid, that provides the plane of tumor spread in laryngeal carcinoma. Parameters: (1) the boundaries - medially the perichondrium of the thyroid lamina, laterally the thyrohyoid membrane inferiorly blending into the cricothyroid membrane, superiorly at the level of the hyoid, inferiorly at the cricoid; (2) the contents - fat and loose connective tissue with lymphatic channels, carrying the recurrent laryngeal nerve and the inferior laryngeal vessels in its lateral part; (3) the relations - the lateral continuation of the pre-epiglottic space, the two together enclosing the larynx; (4) the clinical significance - the plane of spread of T2 laryngeal carcinoma, with invasion of the space, loss of the fat plane on CT or MRI, marking T3 staging. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in head and neck radiology, laryngeal cancer staging, and surgical planning. e.g.: the paraglottic space evaluated on axial CT in AJCC staging of laryngeal carcinoma; paraglottic fat plane loss on MRI marking extralaryngeal extension of a T3 glottic cancer; the paraglottic space opened during a hemilaryngofissure approach in a head and neck surgery atlas | not: the pre-epiglottic space (the anterior compartment bounded by the thyroepiglottic ligament, a distinct compartment); the paralaryngeal space (the lateral neck space outside the larynx, including the strap muscles); the paraglottic perichondrium (the medial boundary, not the space) [formal: spatium paraglotticum | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The stomach is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the muscular sac of the upper abdomen that receives ingested material from the esophagus at the cardiac orifice, stores and mechanically and chemically digests it, and passes chyme to the duodenum at the pyloric orifice. Parameters: (1) the regions — cardia, fundus, body, antrum, and pylorus; (2) the wall layers — mucosa with gastric glands (parietal, chief, and G cells secreting HCl, pepsinogen, and gastrin), submucosa, muscularis externa with oblique, circular, and longitudinal layers, and serosa; (3) the orifices — the cardiac (esophageal) opening superiorly and the pyloric opening inferiorly to the duodenum; (4) the clinical significance — peptic ulcer disease, gastritis, gastric varices, and gastric cancer staging. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, gastroenterology, and surgery. e.g.: the stomach as described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; upper GI endoscopy visualization of the gastric body per the ACG guidelines; barium meal radiograph of the gastric antrum | not: the esophagus (the muscular conduit above, a distinct structure); the small intestine (the tube below, a distinct organ) [formal: gaster | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The cricoarytenoid joint is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the paired synovial joints where the base of each arytenoid cartilage articulates with the superior surface of the cricoid cartilage, whose rotation and sliding movements enable the vocal folds to be abducted, adducted, and adjusted in length and tension. Parameters: (1) the articulation — the cricoarytenoid facet on the base of the arytenoid cartilage against the corresponding facet on the superior surface of the cricoid cartilage; (2) the joint capsule — a thin fibrous capsule enclosing the articular surfaces; (3) the movements — rotation of the arytenoid on a vertical axis through the muscular process (abduction and adduction of the vocal folds) and sliding of the arytenoid base (approximation and lengthening); (4) the muscle action — the posterior cricoarytenoid abducts the fold by rotating the arytenoid, the lateral cricoarytenoid adducts it, and the thyroarytenoid contributes to approximation; (5) the functional outcome — the opening and closing of the glottis and the adjustment of vocal fold length and tension for phonation and airway protection. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, laryngology classification systems, and surgical anatomy references. e.g.: the cricoarytenoid joint described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake; cricoarytenoid joint dislocation following blunt laryngeal trauma per Holinger's classification; the cricoarytenoid joint visualized on axial computed tomography of the larynx in airway evaluation | not: the cricothyroid joint (the articulation between the thyroid inferior horn and the cricoid cartilage); the arytenoid cartilage (the paired cartilage whose base forms one articular surface of the joint); the vocal process (the anterior projection of the arytenoid cartilage that anchors the vocal fold) [formal: articulatio cricoarytenoidea | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The vocal ligament is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the free superior margin of the cricothyroid membrane, forming the elastic fiber core of the vocal fold.
